sources.title: Practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections

indications: Any fluctuant, localised collection of pus.
A perianal abscess: drain it, do not wait for it to point.
A pilonidal abscess, drained off the midline.
Failure of an apparently simple cellulitis to respond, which frequently means an undrained collection.
contraindications: Suspected necrotising soft-tissue infection: this needs urgent theatre and radical debridement, not a bedside incision.
A pulsatile 'abscess', which may be a false aneurysm. Image before incising anything pulsatile.
A collection overlying a joint, a major vessel, or the face in a critical zone, which needs the appropriate specialty.
Inadequate anaesthesia at the bedside is a reason to move to theatre, not a reason to proceed.
preparation: Decide bedside versus theatre honestly: depth, site, size, patient factors and whether adequate anaesthesia is achievable.
Capillary glucose in every patient. An abscess is a common first presentation of diabetes.
Antibiotics are an adjunct, indicated for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features or immunocompromise. They are not the treatment.
Consent to include scarring, incomplete drainage, recurrence, the need for packing and repeat dressings, and for perianal abscess the possibility of a fistula.
positioning: Position so the incision lies at the most dependent point of the cavity.
Lithotomy or prone jack-knife for perianal and pilonidal collections.
Good light and an assistant. Both are underrated.
equipment: Scalpel, forceps, blunt probe or sinus forceps, culture swab or syringe.
Saline for irrigation, and a light dressing or packing material.
Local anaesthetic with a documented maximum safe dose for that patient.
Suction, because a large abscess will spray.
anatomy: The skin overlying an abscess is thinned and inflamed; the true cavity is almost always larger and deeper than the surface suggests.
Perianal abscesses arise from the intersphincteric space and track into perianal, ischiorectal, intersphincteric or supralevator spaces. A horseshoe collection crosses the midline posteriorly.
In the hand and the neck, fascial planes direct spread and confine pus; incisions there need anatomical planning.
Fournier gangrene begins in the perineum and spreads along fascial planes, often with unremarkable overlying skin early on.
criticalSafety: Reconsider the diagnosis in any patient with pain out of proportion, crepitus, dusky skin or systemic toxicity. That is necrotising infection, and this operation is the wrong one.
Break down every loculus. Partial drainage is the commonest reason a patient comes back.
Do not chase a fistula acutely in a perianal abscess; that is an elective decision after the inflammation settles.
structuresAtRisk: Anal sphincter complex in a perianal abscess
Facial nerve branches in a parotid or facial collection
Neurovascular bundles in the limbs and the hand
Named vessels at the base of a deep neck collection
commonErrors: A stab incision too small to keep draining, so the cavity reforms.
Stopping at the first gush of pus without exploring the cavity.
No culture sent, then no way to guide therapy when the patient does not settle.
Tight packing that hurts and causes pressure necrosis.
Missing the diabetic patient, and missing the necrotising infection.
complications: Fistula-in-ano after a perianal abscess, in a substantial minority.
Bleeding, and scarring at a cosmetically important site.
Progression to necrotising infection in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient.
Bacteraemia and sepsis, particularly if drainage is delayed.
postop: Arrange the first dressing change explicitly, and say who will do it.
Antibiotics only where indicated, with a stop date; review the culture when it returns.
Safety-net specifically: increasing pain, spreading redness, fever, or feeling systemically unwell means come straight back.
Arrange follow-up for a pilonidal abscess and a perianal abscess: both need a definitive plan after the acute episode.
Address the underlying cause: glycaemic control, hidradenitis, injecting drug use, immunosuppression.

steps.emphasis: A bedside procedure still gets a check of identity, site, allergy and anticoagulation. The checklist scales down; it does not disappear.
Send the wall of a chronic or atypical abscess for histology as well as culture: tuberculosis and malignancy both present this way.
